newsitem.title: PERU: Peru hostage crisis talks focus on rebels' demand.
newsitem.headline: Peru hostage crisis talks focus on rebels' demand.

text.p: Delicate behind-the-scenes talks in Peru's 117-day hostage crisis focused on the Marxist rebels' demand of freedom for jailed comrades in exchange for their 72 VIP captives, sources close to the talks said.

Roman Catholic Bishop Juan Luis Cipriani, one of a three- man team of guarantors trying overseeing talks, walked into the besieged residence on Saturday afternoon clutching a folder bulging with papers.
He left about an hour later, without the folder and without comment.

Cipriani has carried out a daily shuttle diplomacy this week between President Alberto Fujimori's office and the mined and booby-trapped residence in the rich suburb of San Isidro, looking for a solution to the 16-week siege.
The visit followed a three-hour meeting on Thursday between Cipriani, two other mediators and the leader of the Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) hostage-takers, Nestor Cerpa Cartloini.
To the sound of revolutionary anthems and shouts from the residence, Cerpa was ferried in a white Red Cross car to the talks at a safe house across the street.
It was the first time an MRTA representative had left the house for talks since March 12, when both sides refused to budge on the MRTA's demand for freedom for about 450 jailed comrades.

Fujimori, whom officials say is personally leading the government negotiations with little help from advisers, has publicly ruled out releasing any MRTA prisoners. But sources close to talks said the two sides were haggling over a compromise settlement.

Sources saw no chance of Fujimori agreeing to the release of convicted MRTA fighters. But there was room for possible sentence reductions for low-ranking MRTA prisoners, or release of those detained but not convicted, they said.

"There is a will to reach an agreement," said the same source. He added there may be some ransom payment to the MRTA as part of an overall deal but that "the government does not want to talk about that."
Fujimori has already arranged political asylum for the rebels in Cuba and the Dominican Republic in the event of a peaceful outcome.

About 20 MRTA rebels swept into the Japanese ambassador's home during a cocktail party Dec. 17 and took all 500 guests hostage. They gradually released all but 72 of them, keeping a key list including Peru's foreign minister, Fujimori's brother and top Japanese businessmen.
